To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) Glucagon plays a major regulatory role in hepatic gluconeogenic metabolism in the fetus and newborn rat.

1) the fetus is able to convert lactate into glucose; 2) glucagon is the primary hormone responsible for stimulating gluconeogenesis in the fetal rat; 3) insulin and cortisol are antagonistic hormones to glucagon and inhibit gluconeogenesis in vivo and in vivo; 4) glucose injection causes hypoglycemic suppression of gluconeogenesis and amino acid catabolism; 5) the fetus is not able to convert amino acids into glucose; and
glucagon plays an important role in the induction, and insulin an important role in inhibition of gluconeogenesis during the perinatal period.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of exogenous hormones on plasma levels and on hepatic metabolism of certain amino acids in the fetal and newborn rat.
the regulation of gluco- and lipogenesis from lactate, amino acids and glucose in the fetal and newborn rat.
the role of insulin and glucagon in the regulation of glucose homeostasis in the fetal and newborn rat.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
glucagon plays an important role in the induction and regulation of hepatic gluco- and amino acid-neogenesis in the fetal rat and newborn rat.
the fetal rat liver has an ability to metabolize lactate and amino acid precursors into glucose which is comparable to that of the newborn rat.
the fetal liver is capable of synthesizing glucose from amino acids, but that the process is suppressed in the fetus and newborn rat by high insulin and low glucagon levels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fetal rat has an active gluconeogenic system, which can be activated by glucagon and which is inhibited by insulin.
the newborn animal is in a transitional state in which the fetus is not yet fully adapted to extrauterine life, and the newborn is still not fully able to respond to the extrauterine environment.
glucagon is a potent stimulator of gluconeogenesis in the fetal and newborn rat and that insulin and cortisol act as inhibitors of gluconeogenesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the liver is the major site for the regulation of gluco-neogenesis in the fetus and neonate and that glucagon is the major hormonal stimulus to this process.
glucagon is the major hormonal mediator of gluconeogenesis in the fetus, and that this effect is maintained after birth.

glucagon plays an important role in the induction and regulation of gluconeogenic enzymes in the fetal and newborn liver and that the fetal and newborn rat liver is responsive to the same hormonal influences as the adult liver.
